summary: Monday team meeting with two days left in the month, running about 52 minutes. Opens with wins and a client testimonial Kim relayed from Primal University, then projections: Andrew is $600 to $800 short of a bonus threshold, Richard missed by a distance and is banking on two outstanding deposits, and Kim reports two units from 20 sets at a 75% show rate. Chris releases Kim early and then spends the remaining thirty-five minutes running Objection C, the Open Wallet play, as a live roleplay — first with Andrew, who is corrected for framing payment plans as a certainty rather than as something to be discovered, then demonstrated in full by Chris himself with Richard playing a prospect. The demonstration walks the entire financial picture: monthly surplus, a ninety-day average, discretionary spend, credit cards, available credit, credit score, crypto, precious metals and home equity. It includes an extended reframe aimed at a prospect who refuses debt on principle because of his father's history with credit. Ends with Richard asking Chris directly for an assessment of his performance and getting a 25% close-rate KPI.
notable: Chris teaches a reframe for dismantling a prospect's stated personal refusal to borrow, using the prospect's own family history as the lever: 'Have you ever been to a big city? Well, all those buildings and all that you see? Do you think that the people that own those buildings paid for them in cash?... yes, like maybe your father made some decisions that didn't work out with credit, but that doesn't necessarily mean that credit and loans are bad.' The roleplayed refusal he is answering was 'my dad did, he always up. So I want to be a better father figure for my kids in that sense... if I'm going to take that loan, then I'm just going against my own boundaries.' He follows with 'Just like, what's the fear?'

The financial-picture sequence taught includes home equity, and Chris volunteers the precedent: 'I've had people do it where they'll take, they just decide they want to take equity out on their house, like a little loan or something. You just have to go to the bank.' He then walks it back with 'I probably wouldn't recommend doing that overall.'

Chris recommends steering a prospect toward credit rather than a longer instalment plan, and shows the arithmetic: 'you have a credit card for $5,000 on it... if you put $4,000 down, and then we did a payment plan for the rest, and then you just paid off the card as you go, your payments would be much smaller.'

Richard reports running a full open wallet on a prospect with a negative bank balance and a very low credit score, and intends to collect from him: 'one of them had minus 67 bucks on their accounts', 'his credit score was, like, 400 or 500. Like, what do you even do with that?' and 'I'm gonna follow up with him on Thursday, because that's when he gets some money transfers for the deposit, and then the $1,200 would only be collected the week after.' Chris's response is 'he has not made great financial decisions' and 'if he has negative $67 in his bank account, and he's still planning to move forward and purchase things for $1,000-plus a month, he might be a little impulsive.'

Deposit policy is stated unambiguously for commission purposes and contradicted in practice within the same meeting: 'by the way, it can't be deposited, so they need to at least give you $1,200. Deposits don't count.' Two deposits taken that weekend are nonetheless counted into the week's projections, and Richard notes a separate metric that does count them: 'there's also a stat called call to commitment which takes into account the deposits.'

Chris also coaches genuine restraint, which belongs in the record alongside the rest. He sets a ceiling — 'I try not to take more than 50% to 55% of what they're [left with] at the end of each month' — requires permission before the financial conversation, and instructs reps to talk prospects out of it when it does not work: 'I tell them straight up, I'm like, dude, I don't think you should do this. I don't think this is going to work.' The stated rationale is 'we never want to put anybody in a spot where they got to like sell their couch or something to pay rent.'

The three mandatory elements of the Open Wallet framing per Chris: state that there are no set payment plans and everything is custom, state that you do not want to put them in a rough spot, and explicitly ask permission to have an open conversation about finances. 'Those are the three elements that need to be there. Like a hundred percent need to be there.'

Andrew is corrected for being 'a little cold' and 'so blunt' on money and concedes it: 'The empathy, it's not there when it comes to finances... when it comes to money, I'm like, okay, this is business.'
A euro price appears: Richard quoted a European prospect in dollars and afterwards concluded he should have said '5.2k Euros, that's it' rather than converting from $6,000 on the call.
Richard runs every call through a personal AI tool afterwards: 'after every call, I also run the call through my custom cloud', and cites a specific note it produced about the euro conversion.
Performance standard set: 'Ultimately, KPI is 25%. So I want to see you get your live to call close rate up to 25%', with Chris adding that variance around a 25% average runs 20% to 35%.

Richard took two prospect calls that morning while unwell and says both went badly: 'my energy just wasn't there... my nose is so stuck, and like, I'm a little bit like foggy in my head' and, of the second, 'at the end, my throat was just closing up'.

Richard states a preference for taking unqualified calls as practice: 'I told Kim, like, I still like that he set him, because, well, I'd rather take calls and just not close them, but at least get more practice in.' He also declines to book a further meeting with the negative-balance prospect on the grounds that 'if you have so little money, then I'd rather keep the spot open for someone else'.
Andrew's roleplay character mentions a competitor: 'I did hop on another call with another kettlebell program, and they were about the same price.'

The two outstanding deposits are identifiable from other files in this batch. Richard names Jacob — 'he had to call his bank to increase his credit limit. So I did take a deposit from him on Saturday' — and drafts the follow-up message on screen. He also reports phoning Alan, the 25 June prospect, who asked to be called back Monday, and ends the meeting saying 'I'm gonna call Alan and make sure that deposits it.'

Andrew reports losing a close to a prospect relocating from the UK who wants to start at the end of July; Chris coaches the busy reframe and adds 'Then you're going to find out it's probably a money thing. And if it's a money thing, then you can see if you can work around it and just do the 1200 or whatever you need to do.'
